points.en: Forms eight probing questions on forgiveness, each joining the idea with a different interrogative: who, which, what, why, when, where, how, how much.
Gives a plural noun as the keyword for each question, such as people, kinds, reasons, times, places, ways, amounts.
'Amazing' is an adjective, not a plural noun, so it cannot be a keyword.
A keyword must arise from the probing question; 'why' calls for reasons, so 'amazing' does not come from it.
Corrects it with a plural noun keyword arising from why, such as 'reasons', and a subject like 'reasons grace is amazing'.
States the idea (prayer) and one probing question formed with a single interrogative.
Gives a plural keyword from the question and a subject made of the keyword plus a modifier.
Phrases the objective as an action beginning 'People will...', not a belief.
The plan is coherent and suited to a discouraged congregation.
The keyword names a category, and every point of the outline is a particular instance of that category.
An outline has several parallel points, so the keyword must be plural to hold them; a singular word cannot.
Uses the shelf image: the keyword is the label, the points are the items stored on it.
'Things' is generic and tells the listener almost nothing; it is laziness, not a keyword.
A keyword should be as specific as possible to the content of the divisions, so the sermon has a definite shape.
Gives examples of specific keywords such as reasons, ways, dangers or examples.
Gives a subject with 'ways' modified by an adjective, such as 'effective ways'.
Gives a subject with 'ways' modified by a prepositional phrase, such as 'ways of gaining faith'.
Gives a subject with 'ways' modified by a subordinate clause, such as 'ways that God speaks'.
'Understand' names a belief or attitude, not an action, so it is weak as an objective.
The rewrite is a concrete action that could be measured, phrased as 'People will...'.
Actions bring beliefs along, but informed beliefs do not always lead to action.
Forms probing questions on love using different interrogatives, showing each yields a different sermon.
Chooses a probing question for Mother's Day and ties the choice to the occasion.
Chooses a probing question for Good Friday and ties the choice to the occasion, such as the cross.
States the idea (patience) and one probing question using a single interrogative.
Derives a plural keyword from that question.
Writes a subject made of the keyword plus a modifier.
Phrases the objective as a concrete action beginning 'People will...'.
'Know' names a belief, not an action, so the objective cannot be seen or measured.
Rewrites it as a concrete, measurable action beginning 'People will...'.
Actions carry beliefs with them, but informed beliefs do not always produce action.
